Here is a quick and dependable recipe for classic fudgy brownies. You only need one bowl and a few kitchen staples.

Ingredients

1/2 cup (115g) Unsalted butter, melted1 cup (200g) Granulated sugar2 Large eggs1 tsp Vanilla extract1/3 cup (35g) Cocoa powder1/2 cup (65g) All-purpose flour1/4 tsp Salt1/2 cup Chocolate chips (optional)

Step-by-Step Instructions

Preheat and Prep: Heat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Line an 8x8-inch baking pan with parchment paper.

Mix Wet Ingredients: Whisk the melted butter and sugar together in a medium bowl. Add the eggs and vanilla, then whisk vigorously until the mixture looks pale and smooth.

Fold in Dry Ingredients: Sift in the cocoa powder, flour, and salt. Stir gently with a spatula just until combined. Do not overmix.

Add Mix-ins: Fold in the chocolate chips if you are using them.

Bake: Pour the batter into your pan and smooth the top. Bake for 20 to 22 minutes. A toothpick inserted into the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, but no wet batter.

Cool and Slice: Let them cool completely in the pan before slicing.

text:
Really appreciated this vid. 
A ton to discuss here, but will give the tldr version: This reads like a demo in place of a commercial; instead of investing in ad space, they opted for an event.
Cool engineering, but outside of scaling the technologies are (admittedly in broad strokes) largely refinements of existing technologies that are just barely packaged into a “car”. This car is more like a cool engineering fever dream than something most folks would actually describe as a true “flying car”. 
Two innovations/observations Tesla has highlighted- 1) It takes time, and well-researched pricing to establish as a new luxury brand (model S was a master class in this, and positioning and timing were excellent); 2) Unique marketing; they take a tech company approach to marketing (expo-style event-based demos/reveals) over traditional commercials, ad banners, etc.

author: @JosefHelmut
text:
I live in a smart home. Every light is smart. Every lock is smart. Several fans, the thermostat, and a small choir of HomePods scattered through the house are all smart. The weak link is me, because I'm an Apple ecosystem guy. In practice that means saying "Hey Siri, turn off the kitchen lights" three times, in rising tones of desperation, until the lights finally take pity on me or I give up and live in the glow.

What I needed was a control panel. Actually, several of them, placed strategically around the house. Voice commands aren't always an option, and my house guests don't know that the lamp in the corner answers to "Living Room Accent 2." Without a panel, a visitor's choices are to stand in the dark or shout guesses at the ceiling like they're summoning a ghost.

So I built my own. I bought two used iPad minis and stripped them down to the Home app and the Ring app. I set up a screen anyone can use to turn things on and off: no Face ID, no passcode, no "Sorry, I didn't catch that." I tap a button and the light turns on. It's revolutionary stuff.

I kept hoping Apple would see the obvious and make real control tablets in two sizes: a big one to run the whole house, and small ones in each room for that room's devices. Physical light switches are on their way out, and somebody has to replace them.

Then Apple finally announced its answer: an iPad glued onto a HomePod mini, with FaceTime.

FaceTime.

I already have FaceTime on my iPhone, both iMacs, and my iPad. If anything, I'm over-FaceTimed. Recipes? My little kitchen iPad on its stand has that covered, and it doesn't want a medal for it.

Then there's the wall-mounted version. It costs the same as the regular one, and you buy the mounting hardware separately. So I'd pay full price for the privilege of screwing it into my own wall.

I honestly don't know what they were thinking. It's a gimmick dressed up as a tool. I'll keep my Frankenstein iPad minis, which at least do the one thing I need, every time, on the first try. That's more than I can say for Siri.

video_title: Dear YouTube!
author: @Zelijahrs
text:
This seems to me like the clearest cut example of a fundamental misunderstanding of the value of shared truth and knowledge in our society, especially amongst the tech community. We've been seeing this for a while with those pushing AI at Google and myopic maximization of short term gains. Something like this would never be pushed by an actual media organization like the New York Times, NPR, NBC, etc. And a lot of the people who were pioneers in the tech industry lauded those very same liberal values as things that the internet would champion. This is why we have the internet archive. This is how Google was supposed to help you research. And until now and recently, this has been one of the main values of YouTube: a massive communication platform that is more about people putting out original and detailed ideas than about them engaging in short-term arguments or agitation. 

If there is no record-keeping methodology launched with this feature for you to be able to view different archival versions of the video, track what you have shared to people and what is being watched, then there will be a massive issue for the credibility of our conversations. 

This comes at a period of time when, unfortunately, YouTube is taking on a larger and larger role in the information sphere. It tends to be less volatile than somewhere like Twitter, TikTok, or any of the meta platforms due to the level of work involved in posting something and the sustained nature of the community that follows an individual speaker. Further, Youtube has become one of the number one places for people to receive news, as more and more podcasts ranging from professional outlets like the New York Times and NPR, to scrappy upstarts, to fringe theorists, often come here to both post their content and engage with others on what they believe is happening in the world. Those opinions need to be trackable, traceable, and referenceable.

It's a core tenant of information theory in a democracy. And without that traceability in one of the major domains of communication, we are at a much greater risk for being able to effectively communicate with one another about misinformation and about our world. Not to mention the amount of misinformation it creates on its own and the fact that this is a license for other platforms to continue doing the same thing or to start doing it even if they hadn't considered it.

video_title: Dear YouTube!
author: @justinflom
text:
I usually really align with your hot takes, but I have a different perspective here. I’m a creator, and my job is to come up with interesting ideas and present them to the most people possible. But the truth is, I don’t always know how to best communicate that idea.

A stand-up comic goes onstage night after night, editing and rewriting his material based on the audience response. He’s not changing his artistic vision or his beliefs to suit an audience. He’s finding the best way to communicate his original idea so the audience receives it.

Example: I built a loft above the stairs in my house, and it was a crazy project. Expensive, time-consuming, and I knew I really only had one shot to get the video right when I posted it organically to YouTube Shorts. So I edited what I thought was the best version and tested it with a Facebook ad shown to 10,000 people. It got very low retention. Oh no.
I did this again 40 times, editing and testing until I found a radically different way of presenting the idea. That video ended up with over 150 million views on Shorts. If I’d just posted my original edit, data says it wouldn't have broken one million.

I’ve been lobbying YouTube for years to give us something like Trial Reels on Instagram, so that by the time a video gets to our subscribers, it’s the best possible video it can be. YouTube told me their biggest concern with a tool like this was bad actors taking advantage of it. I totally understand that, and I understand your concerns. Maybe the tool could have been built differently. I would have preferred a way to test content with non-subscribers before showing it to subscribers (the people I care about). That said, I’m always excited to learn how to better present creative, original ideas to an audience.

text:
"As a viewer, do I know if the video I'm watching is part of an A/B test?"
Nope! You have zero clue. You are just a blind data point feeding the almighty algorithm.

"If I'm reading the comments, how do I know which version of the video they watched?"
You don't! Nobody does! Even the creator won't know which cut a commenter is yapping about. It’s going to turn the comment section into a digital insane asylum where everyone is arguing about a completely different reality.

"Will comment timestamps break if I'm watching the other version?"
Oh, 110% yes. If the cuts are different lengths, clicking a timestamp will just drop you into a random, confusing void. So much for finding the best part of a video!

"How long after publishing can creators test a video?"
Only at the launch of a new video. Thank god they at least had the microscopic amount of sense to realize you shouldn't be allowed to go back and constantly replace your old uploads.

"If I send a video to someone, could they end up watching a completely different video than the one I saw?"
Yup! You could watch one version, send the link to a friend, and by the time they click it, YouTube has declared a different version the "winner." You won't even be sharing the same experience.

"How different are the tested videos actually allowed to be?"
YouTube claims they are building a "semantic analysis model"—which is just corporate speak for an AI bot—to scan both video files and give them a "similarity score." If they aren't similar enough, they can't be tested. But considering AI still struggles to count the number of fingers on a human hand, I’m sure this will work flawlessly.

text:
As a viewer, I feel like answering the question of "Have I already watched this video?" should be mundanely trivial. (And "Did you see the same video that I did?" even more so.) Thumbnail and title A/B testing has already frustrated that determination at the expense of fast-tracking the insight that creators once had to gather by just committing to decisions and learning from them.

Also, with YouTube views now calculated at the first frame's generation, what would stop any creator from just "A/B testing" three different intros to maximize view count during the honeymoon period by making it impossible to know if you've seen a video before? Or A/B testing three different thumbnails, titles, and video segments simultaneously? As you said, optimizing for performance through quantifiable metrics really seems to undercut the community experience and creative expressions that make YouTube unique.

text: In most of the situations these watches will actually be used for, the wearer is a participant in the conversation. The large majority of U.S. states and federal law are one-party consent, so the wearer doesn’t need the other people’s permission to record a conversation they’re part of. Separately, the statutes only protect communications where there’s a reasonable expectation of privacy. Loud public ambient sound usually doesn’t qualify. That doesn’t erase every privacy concern people have about always-listening devices, but the framing that this is illegal wiretapping in most of America doesn’t hold up. It’s also hard to ignore that governments, platforms, and advertising companies have run detailed surveillance on nearly every aspect of our lives for years. The sudden volume of concern only seems to spike once the same kind of technology starts giving regular users a direct personal benefit.

It’s also hard to ignore that governments, platforms, and advertising companies have run detailed surveillance on nearly every aspect of our lives for years. The sudden volume of concern only seems to spike once the same kind of technology starts giving regular users a direct personal benefit.

text: There is a market for this. Hemory already runs continuous listening on the Apple Watch, and it hit #1 day rank on Product Hunt. It even goes further than Apple, since it keeps full text transcripts in the cloud. Most US states allow one-party consent, where a participant can record a conversation. So Apple could limit these features to those states, based on where the watch is, not where the user lives. Apple could also require voice enrollment, so the watch only processes conversations where the user speaks. That does not solve everything. Voice enrollment cannot prove the user took part in every conversation in hearing range, and a voiceprint is biometric data with its own laws. But it would move the feature closer to "a conversation the user took part in" and away from eavesdropping. The difference between long-running tools and ones like Granola, ideashell, or a voice memo is the scope of the decision. With a voice memo, one tap covers one conversation, and the user knows who is in it. With Hemory or Siri Recap, one tap or one opt-in covers a whole day of conversations (or more) the user has not had yet. So the user no longer decides per conversation. Legally, "I forgot to turn it off" may even help the user, since most wiretap laws need intent. That pushes the responsibility toward the vendor that designed the default.

And apparently…

It worked again.

Until next year, Apple.

One thing all reviewers missed....
The Aluminum Radiator: The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8's Armor Aluminum frame has a thermal conductivity rate roughly 10 times higher than the Apple iPhone Duo’s Grade 5 Titanium. Even though graphite sheets move heat away from the processor slightly slower than a vapor chamber, the aluminum frame is incredibly efficient at dumping that heat out into the open air.

The "Cool-to-the-Touch" Fallacy: If a reviewer holds the iPhone Duo and it feels cooler in their hands during a brief play session, they often praise its cooling. They don't realize that the titanium frame is simply trapping the heat inside, protecting their fingers while baking the processor and battery.

text:
The 10,000 Nits / 165Hz Myth: Chasing these specs is literal suicide for a 5,700 mAh battery. A phone isn't built to sustain 10k nits without aggressive thermal throttling. Samsung needs to be conservative here: 3,000 nits peak and 144Hz is the ultimate sweet spot for fluid gaming and outdoor visibility.
2️⃣ The Privacy Display Math: Privacy filters naturally cut down light transmittance by roughly 400 nits. If Samsung targets a 3,000 nits base panel, enabling the privacy mode drops it to a perfect 2,600 nits. The genius part? Users get total privacy while maintaining the exact same flagship brightness as the S26 Ultra's normal mode. Zero quality complaints.
3️⃣ Fix the Colors, Drop the Gimmicks: The Ultra line is a beast, but it desperately needs a boost in color vividness on both the front and rear cameras. Stripping it too natural makes it look washed out next to the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Everyday users want vibrant, punchy colors that pop on social media. Also, dropping the 3x physical lens to fit that 5,700 mAh silicon-carbon battery is smart, but the 200MP computational crop from 3x to 4.9x must be flawless.
4️⃣ Use the Free Space Wisely: Removing a camera lens frees up crucial internal real estate. Don't just leave it there. Samsung must expand the Vapor Chamber to handle the raw power of the new 2nm chip, optimize weight distribution so it doesn't feel top-heavy, and embed strong native magnetic rings under the back glass.
Raw specs on paper mean nothing if the phone thermal throttles in 3 minutes. Usability and balance are everything. What do you guys think? 🚀

text:
Pixel 11 Pro XL won't connect to my Škoda Kamiq — and Google still has no solution

I'm a long-time Pixel user. I've owned the Pixel 4, 5, 6 and 7, and I recently decided to upgrade to the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Unfortunately, I've had a major problem with the phone that I consider unacceptable: Android Auto will not connect to my 2023 Škoda Kamiq via USB.

What's particularly frustrating is that Android Auto worked perfectly in this exact car with both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and iPhone Air, using a cable.

What I've tried

When I first switched to the Pixel 11 Pro XL, Android Auto simply wouldn't connect.

I contacted Google Support and went through all the troubleshooting they instructed me to do. None of it worked.

Google then suggested contacting my Škoda dealer because information circulating on Reddit suggested that the infotainment firmware in some Škoda/VW vehicles might be responsible.

I contacted Škoda. They told me that, according to their system, my Kamiq already has the latest available firmware. They said that if I wanted further investigation, I would need to take the car to a dealership and pay approximately AUD $250 for an investigation.

I wasn't prepared to pay $250 to investigate an unconfirmed theory, particularly when I had another way to test whether the car itself was actually the problem.

The Pixel 7 test

I tested my friend's Pixel 7 in my Kamiq, using the same car and connection.

It connected to Android Auto perfectly.

That was a very important result for me.

The car clearly supports Android Auto, and the USB connection works. A previous iPhone worked. Another Pixel works.

The problem appears to be specifically related to the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

I explained this to Google Support and told them that I shouldn't have to become the middleman between Google and Škoda to get a new Google phone to work with Android Auto.

Google acknowledged that there was an issue affecting the Pixel and told me to wait for the September update, which I was told would resolve the problem.

I agreed to wait.

I tried AAWireless as a workaround

While waiting, I purchased an AAWireless adapter so I could at least use Android Auto wirelessly.

Initially, it worked reasonably well.

Unfortunately, yesterday it became extremely unreliable. During my drive it was repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting approximately every 30 seconds.

That is not an acceptable situation for something I'm using while driving, particularly because I rely heavily on navigation.

I don't consider a third-party wireless adapter an adequate solution to a phone that cannot establish a reliable wired Android Auto connection in the first place.

The September update didn't solve it

After receiving the September update, I tested the phone again.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL still would not connect to Android Auto via USB.

I contacted Google Support again.

This time I was told that the engineering team is aware of the problem, but there is currently no timeframe for when it will be resolved.

At this point, I can't keep waiting indefinitely.

I've decided to try to return the phone.

What frustrates me most

I'm a Pixel fan. I've owned multiple generations of Pixel phones despite experiencing various bugs over the years.

But this situation is different.

I rely heavily on navigation when driving, so reliable Android Auto connectivity isn't a minor convenience for me. A connection that repeatedly fails or disconnects while driving can become a safety issue.

I also find it unreasonable that the customer is being placed between two manufacturers:

Google: “Contact your car manufacturer.”

Škoda: “Your car has the latest firmware. Pay approximately $250 for further investigation.”

Google: “Our engineering team knows about the issue, but we can't tell you when it will be fixed.”

Meanwhile, the customer has a brand-new flagship phone that cannot perform a basic function that their previous phone performed perfectly.

About the Škoda firmware theory

There is information on Reddit suggesting that certain Škoda/VW infotainment firmware versions may have compatibility problems with newer Pixel phones.

ChatGPT and Gemini also tend to suggest updating the vehicle's infotainment firmware when asked about similar Android Auto problems, and this possibility was even referenced during my interactions with Google Support.

However, I have not found official confirmation from Google or Škoda/VW that my particular issue can be resolved by updating the car's firmware.

That's an important distinction.

I don't think customers should be expected to spend hundreds of dollars investigating an unofficial theory, especially when a Pixel 7 works perfectly in the same car.

My question to Google

If a car is equipped with Android Auto and is working correctly with other compatible phones, shouldn't a new Android phone be expected to connect to it reliably without the customer having to get caught between the phone manufacturer and the car manufacturer?

I understand that compatibility issues can happen. What I don't understand is why the responsibility for resolving them is being pushed back and forth between Google and Škoda while the customer is left without a solution.

A flagship phone should be fit for purpose.

For me, that includes reliably connecting to Android Auto in a vehicle that supports Android Auto.

I've now reached the point where I don't want to keep troubleshooting, buying third-party accessories or waiting for an unspecified future update. I just want a phone that works with my car.

It's a shame because I've been a Pixel customer for years, and I genuinely wanted to stay with Pixel.

But when driving safety and navigation are involved, “we're aware of the problem, but we can't tell you when it will be fixed” isn't good enough.

This obsession with extreme specs and niche features needs to stop dominating phone reviews. For many people, a Pixel is an everyday phone, and being a phone enthusiast doesn’t automatically mean being a hardcore mobile gamer.

Photos from my old Pixel 8 often look better to me than those from my Galaxy S26 Ultra. By “better,” I mean the processing delivers a pleasing, finished image that’s ready to upload to social media without editing. That point-and-shoot experience matters, and it doesn’t always show up on a spec sheet.

Gaming performance deserves scrutiny, but so do camera consistency, battery life, connectivity, and smooth everyday use. The Pixel should absolutely be judged on its weaknesses and its price, but being less suited to demanding games shouldn’t automatically make it a phone for “non-enthusiasts.” Different enthusiasts value different things.

"Budget" Phones: Cost Ksh 50,000 – 80,000 (~$380 – $600 USD). There are zero trade-in options for this tier, making long-term value hard to justify.
Flagships: Cost Ksh 110,000+ (~$850+ USD). However, local trade-ins only exist for Apple, Samsung, and Google.

My Dilemma:
Should I buy a mid-ranger and eat 100% of the depreciation, or buy a flagship knowing I can actually trade it in years down the line?
I am strongly leaning toward the Google Pixel Pro line because I want a clean software experience and a normal-sized form factor (the Galaxy Ultra is too massive and have never used iphone before). Given my need for a 7-year lifespan and the strange trade-in economy in East Africa.
Would you recommend the Pixel Pro, or should I look at something else entirely?

Would love to hear your thoughts!

I've switched to Samsung this year, and I'm genuinely rooting for them. I want them to succeed because competition is good. But the more I use it, the more I realize Apple's biggest advantage has never been hardware—it's the software experience.

Samsung wins on paper with specs, but it's the little things that make Apple feel more complete. Features like the charging dock mode, polished UI, seamless wallpapers and themes, and all the small quality-of-life touches add up. It feels like Samsung is trying to beat Apple on hardware when software is where the real gap still exists.

That said, Apple isn't perfect either. Their file transfer system has always been frustrating. Instead of embracing open standards like Bluetooth, they've pushed users toward AirDrop and their own ecosystem. On top of that, you have to buy the expensive Pro models to get many of the headline features.

For now, I'm sticking with Samsung because I want to explore what Android has to offer. The Z Fold 8 looks interesting, but software is still my biggest concern. If Samsung doesn't convince me, I might give the Pixel Pro a try next year.

Классические домашние сырники получаются нежными, с румяной корочкой и мягкой серединкой.

Ингредиенты

• Творог (5–9% жирности) — 400 г (лучше брать сухой или умеренно влажный)
• Яйцо — 1 шт.
• Сахар — 2 ст. ложки
• Ванильный сахар — 10 г (или щепотка ванилина)
• Соль — 1 щепотка
• Пшеничная мука — 1–2 ст. ложки (в тесто) + мука для панировки
• Растительное масло — для жарки

Пошаговый рецепт

1. Подготовьте творог: Выложите творог в миску и разомните вилкой. Если в нем много крупных крупинок, можно перетереть его через сито, тогда текстура будет более однородной.
2. Смешайте основу: Добавьте к творогу яйцо, сахар, ванильный сахар и щепотку соли. Тщательно перемешайте массу вилкой или лопаткой.
3. Добавьте муку: Всыпьте 1–2 столовые ложки муки. Аккуратно перемешайте. Постарайтесь не добавлять лишней муки, иначе сырники станут «забитыми» и жесткими.
4. Сформируйте сырники: Присыпьте чистый стол или доску мукой. Слегка влажными руками берите порции теста, скатывайте в шарики, а затем аккуратно приплющивайте их в плоские шайбы толщиной около 1,5–2 см. Слегка обваляйте каждую заготовку в муке со всех сторон.
5. Обжарьте: Хорошо разогрейте сковороду с растительным маслом на среднем огне. Выложите сырники и жарьте около 3–4 минут до появления красивой золотистой корочки.
6. Доведите до готовности: Переверните сырники на другую сторону. Сделайте огонь чуть тише, накройте сковороду крышкой и готовьте еще 2–3 минуты, чтобы они полностью пропеклись внутри.
7. Подача: Выложите готовые сырники на бумажное полотенце, чтобы впиталось лишнее масло. Подавайте теплыми со сметаной, медом или любимым вареньем.

IF A DOCTOR HAD 150 DAYS TO FOCUS ON NOTHING BUT EARNING A PLACE IN HER DREAM SPECIALTY… HOW FAR COULD SHE GO?


Hi MrBeast Team!!


I’m Zeynep, a young doctor from Türkiye. And I’m pitching you a video whose ending even I don’t know:

“We Gave a Doctor 150 Days to Achieve Her Dream!”

My dream is to become a child and adolescent psychiatrist. To get there, I need a very high score on the TUS, Türkiye’s medical specialty entrance exam.

Ahead of me are months of preparation, limited places, and an exam where even a small difference in scores could change my future.

Here’s my proposal:

Give me a home to live in until the exam, the study resources I need, and the support to focus without worrying about everyday expenses. Set up the cameras. On day one, I’ll take a practice exam so everyone can see exactly where I’m starting.

Then let the countdown begin.

150 days.
A new practice exam every week.
A score that changes on screen.
The real exam getting closer.

Viewers can see how close I’m getting to my goal. If I improve one week and fall behind the next, they’ll see that too. They’ll watch me change course when my plan stops working and find a way forward on the difficult days.

We could add medical knowledge duels with specialists, clinical case challenges, and weekly milestones. But one question would remain at the heart of it all:

“Will Zeynep make it?”

When the day comes, I’ll step away from the cameras and sit the real exam.

You won’t choose the questions.
I won’t control my score.
We’ll all have to wait for the results.

And eventually, we’ll find out whether the goal everyone has watched me work toward becomes an actual place in my dream specialty.

For me, it means seeing my name next to the specialty I’ve wanted for years.

For your team, it’s a story with a starting point, a countdown, measurable progress, and a genuinely uncertain outcome.

I can’t guarantee success. But I can commit to sharing my pursuit of this dream with complete honesty.

I’m ready to share my baseline score, preparation plan, and a short introduction video.

When are we filming the first practice exam?

Zeynep
A doctor from Türkiye

Someone is reading this in bed.
Someone is in a hospital.
Someone is in school.
Someone is in a car. Someone is in the metro.

Different lives. Different places.

But if you're reading this, and you can breathe air in... and out...
You are still here. 🤍

Maybe your alarm annoyed you this morning.
Someone else woke up afraid of what today would bring.

Maybe you complained about the same food again?
Somewhere, a parent is wondering how to tell their child there's no dinner tonight.

Maybe traffic was slow? The bus was crowded? The walk was long?
But you... you reached home.
Don't forget that part. You reached home.

Maybe your mom called while you were busy.
Maybe your dad asked the same question twice.
If you still have them... give them a little time.
Some people only have old messages left to read.

So tonight, if you turn a key, open a door, and hear someone say "You're home"...
Stop. Take a second.

An ordinary day brought you back to each other.
That is worth noticing.

If this found you today, it was meant for you. 🤍
